Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in the tumor microenvironment where IL-6 and TNF-α are abundantly present, these cytokines activate specific PTM enzymes, such as JAK1 for phosphorylation and glycosyltransferases (e.g., STT3A), which in turn mediate precise glycosylation and phosphorylation events on CLDN18.2. These modifications lead to the disruption of tight junction architecture and the unveiling of new epitopes on the extracellular domain of CLDN18.2. The newly exposed binding interfaces are hypothesized to enhance the recognition and efficacy of CLDN18.2-directed immunotherapies. To test this, we will employ cutting-edge strategies including high-resolution mass spectrometry for mapping PTM sites, CRISPR-based screens to validate the involvement of candidate enzymes, and machine learning algorithms to analyze proteomic changes and predict structural shifts. Pharmacological agents aimed at modulating these PTMs will be evaluated for their capacity to further improve immunotherapeutic outcomes, offering a novel avenue for cancer treatment.
Abstract: This study proposes that in the inflammatory milieu of solid tumors, elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-α drive a cascade of post-translational modifications (PTMs) on the tight junction protein CLDN18.2. Specifically, these cytokines activate PTM enzymes—including kinases such as JAK1 and candidate glycosyltransferases like STT3A—leading to precise phosphorylation and glycosylation of CLDN18.2. This modification is hypothesized to disrupt tight junction integrity, thereby reconfiguring the extracellular domain to expose novel binding epitopes. By integrating machine learning-assisted proteomic profiling, high-resolution imaging, and CRISPR-based functional screens, our approach aims to both identify these specific modifications and validate the causative relationship between cytokine signaling and CLDN18.2 structural alterations. Pharmacological modulation of these PTMs is anticipated to enhance the binding and efficacy of CLDN18.2-directed immunotherapies, such as monoclonal antibodies and CAR-T cells, ultimately improving anti-tumor responses.
CausalChain: High inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-6, TNF-α) -> Activation of PTM-specific enzymes (JAK1, glycosyltransferases including STT3A) -> Induction of site-specific glycosylation and phosphorylation on CLDN18.2 -> Disruption of tight junction integrity and enhanced exposure of novel epitopes -> Altered binding interfaces on CLDN18.2 -> Improved engagement of CLDN18.2-directed immunotherapies
